issues.legal_issue: A state legislature lacks competence to create a statutory appeal directly to the Supreme Court from a state rent tribunal.
material_facts: The state legislature enacted a rent-control law regulating landlord-tenant relations and providing for adjudication by a Rent Controller and an appellate Rent Control Tribunal.
The law also provided a statutory appeal from an order of the Tribunal directly to the Supreme Court.
The law had received the President’s assent.
The appeal raised the constitutional validity of the provision for a direct appeal.
issues.conclusion: The state legislature was competent to legislate on tenancy and rent and to establish the rent-control adjudication structure, but lacked competence to provide a statutory appeal to the Supreme Court. The direct-appeal provision was declared ultra vires, null and void, and of no effect.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 245 and 246 allocate legislative authority according to the Seventh Schedule. Entry 18 of the State List supports state legislation on land, landlord-tenant relations and rent; Article 323B permits an appropriate legislature to provide for tenancy and rent tribunals. But Entry 77 of the Union List assigns legislation concerning the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction and powers to Parliament, while Entry 65 of the State List and Entry 46 of the Concurrent List exclude the Supreme Court from their grant of authority concerning courts. Article 323B(3)(d) permits exclusion of court jurisdiction subject to the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction under Article 136, but does not authorize a state legislature to add a statutory appeal to the Supreme Court. The ancillary-powers principle in United Provinces v. Atika Begum does not make such an appeal incidental to the state’s power over tenancy. The Court agreed with H.S. Yadav v. Shakuntala Devi Parakh.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_state_law: A party challenged the constitutional validity of a state-law provision in court.
predicates.state_legislature_created_direct_statuto: A state legislature enacted a provision requiring an appeal from a tribunal to be brought directly to the Supreme Court.
predicates.appeal_changes_supreme_court_jurisdictio: The provision purports to add a statutory appellate function to the Supreme Court.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a state legislature’s provision adding a direct statutory appeal to the Supreme Court, the provision is invalid if it changes the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: Presidential assent does not cure a state enactment that the state legislature lacked competence to make.
material_facts: The state legislature enacted the provision for a statutory appeal directly to the Supreme Court.
The President assented to the state law after it was reserved for consideration.
The provision concerned the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction, an area outside the state legislature’s legislative authority.
issues.conclusion: Presidential assent could not validate the provision because the state legislature lacked competence to enact it.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 200 and 201 govern presentation, reservation and assent of state Bills, but assent does not enlarge a legislature’s constitutional competence. K.K. Poonacha v. State of Karnataka establishes that presidential assent does not immunize a state enactment that is outside the state legislature’s competence or otherwise constitutionally invalid. Assent may cure repugnancy with an earlier central statute where the state legislature is otherwise competent; it cannot cure legislative incompetence.

predicates.state_legislature_lacked_competence: The state legislature enacted a provision on a subject outside the legislative authority assigned to it.
predicates.president_assented_to_state_law: The President assented to the state law after it was presented or reserved for consideration.

issues.definition: If a state legislature enacts a provision outside its legislative authority, presidential assent does not make that provision valid.

issues.legal_issue: Presidential assent to a state Bill is not a special agreement conferring additional jurisdiction on the Supreme Court, and an enabling parliamentary law is also required.
material_facts: The state Bill was reserved for the President and received presidential assent.
The appellant argued that assent, given on the advice of the Union Council of Ministers, amounted to an agreement between the Union and the state to confer appellate jurisdiction.
There was no independent agreement reached through deliberations and negotiations between the Union and the state.
Parliament had not enacted a law providing for the Supreme Court to exercise the proposed additional jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The requirements for conferring additional jurisdiction under Article 138(2) were not met; presidential assent was neither the required special agreement nor a substitute for an enabling parliamentary law.
issues.legal_principle: Article 138(2) permits additional Supreme Court jurisdiction concerning any matter to be conferred by special agreement between the Government of India and a state government, provided Parliament by law provides for the exercise of that jurisdiction. A President’s assent to a state law, even when given on ministerial advice, is not an independent agreement between the governments and does not dispense with the parliamentary-law requirement.

predicates.additional_supreme_court_jurisdiction_is: A state enactment purports to give the Supreme Court an additional form of jurisdiction.
predicates.only_presidential_assent_was_given: The state Bill received presidential assent, without a separate agreement between the governments.
predicates.no_independent_intergovernmental_agreeme: The national and state governments did not reach a separate agreement through deliberations and negotiations to confer the jurisdiction.
predicates.no_enabling_parliamentary_law: Parliament did not enact a law providing for the Supreme Court to exercise the proposed jurisdiction.

issues.definition: A proposed additional jurisdiction is not conferred when the only step taken is presidential assent and there is neither an independent agreement between the governments nor an enabling parliamentary law.

issues.legal_issue: The discretionary special-leave jurisdiction of the Supreme Court does not make a separate statutory right of appeal to that Court an incidental extension of existing jurisdiction.
material_facts: The state law purported to give a party a statutory second appeal to the Supreme Court from the Rent Control Tribunal.
The appellant argued that the provision merely extended or reflected the Supreme Court’s existing jurisdiction to grant special leave.
The statutory provision required an appeal to be considered even where the tribunal decisions involved concurrent findings and no serious question of law.
issues.conclusion: The statutory appeal was distinct from the Supreme Court’s discretionary special-leave jurisdiction and could not be justified as an extension of that jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: Article 136 gives the Supreme Court discretionary power to grant special leave; it does not confer a right of appeal. N. Natarajan v. B.K. Subba Rao recognizes the discretionary character of that power, and Dhakeshwari Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income Tax confirms that statutory finality does not bar its exercise. A statutory appeal, by contrast, requires the appellate court to hear the case and review errors of fact and law. The existence of Article 136 therefore does not authorize a state legislature to create a separate mandatory statutory appeal to the Supreme Court.

predicates.state_law_creates_mandatory_supreme_cour: A state enactment requires an appeal to the Supreme Court to be heard as a statutory appeal.
predicates.appeal_is_claimed_to_be_only_special_lea: A party argues that the statutory appeal is merely an exercise or extension of the Supreme Court’s discretionary power to grant special leave.

issues.definition: A mandatory statutory appeal created by state law remains distinct from discretionary special-leave jurisdiction, even when a party characterizes it as an extension of that jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: The constitutional restriction requiring reservation of a Bill that endangers the High Court’s constitutional position is not engaged merely because a statute provides no appeal to the High Court.
material_facts: The state law provided for a tribunal appeal and a direct statutory appeal to the Supreme Court, but did not remove the High Court’s powers of judicial review under Articles 226 and 227.
The appellant argued that presidential assent under the second proviso to Article 200 could support the statutory appeal provision.
The Court found that the provision did not derogate from a power of the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The second proviso to Article 200 was not attracted because the provision did not derogate from the High Court’s powers; the absence of a statutory appeal to the High Court did not itself trigger the proviso.
issues.legal_principle: The second proviso to Article 200 requires the Governor to reserve a Bill if, in the Governor’s opinion, it would so derogate from the High Court’s powers as to endanger the position the Constitution gives that Court. A statutory right of appeal is not inherent, and a statute is not invalid merely because it provides no appeal to the High Court. The High Court’s powers under Articles 226 and 227 remain protected as an inviolable basic feature under L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, but that protection does not turn those powers into ordinary appellate jurisdiction.

predicates.state_law_provides_no_high_court_statuto: A state law does not provide a statutory appeal to the High Court from the relevant tribunal decision.
predicates.high_court_constitutional_review_powers_: The law leaves the High Court’s constitutional judicial-review powers in place.

issues.definition: The absence of a statutory appeal to the High Court does not trigger the reservation requirement when the law leaves the High Court’s constitutional review powers untouched.
